claims.text: Gmail's bulk sender requirements apply once a domain sends about 5,000 messages a day to personal Gmail accounts: SPF and DKIM, a DMARC record (a policy of none is enough), a From domain that aligns with one of them, one-click unsubscribe on marketing mail, and a spam rate under 0.3%.

A small SaaS is usually far below 5,000 a day, but Google counts every subdomain under your main domain together and never lets a domain drop back out, so the cheap move is to meet the bulk rules from your first email.
Of the 119 that handle email at all, 42 (35%) publish no DMARC record, the bulk-only requirement anyone can check from outside.

| Rule | Gmail | Yahoo | Outlook.com | |---|---|---|---| | Who counts as bulk | About 5,000+ a day to personal Gmail accounts, per primary domain; permanent once reached | No number given | Over 5,000 a day to outlook.com, hotmail.com and live.com | | Everyone: authentication | SPF or DKIM | SPF or DKIM | No rule below 5,000 | | Everyone: other | Forward and reverse DNS, TLS, RFC 5322 format, spam
- The bulk threshold. Google and Microsoft both say 5,000 a day, but Google counts per primary domain: its FAQ's example adds promotions.solarmora.com to solarmora.com.

Yahoo never gives a number, which is the practical argument for meeting the bulk rules at any volume. - The spam rate. Our plan for this post noted that the "0.3%" figure kept turning up only on email vendors' blogs.
It is in Google's own pages: 0.3% is the limit in the requirements, and the guidelines add that you should stay below 0.1% and never reach 0.3%.
Above 0.3%, the FAQ says Google offers no mitigation until the rate has stayed under it for seven days in a row.
Yahoo also says 0.3% and computes it on mail that reached the inbox.

At least 62 of the 113 mail domains without wildcard DNS (55%) have a key at one of the 12 names we tried, most often google (29) and resend (20).
